newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OK for Boeing-McDonnell merger seen next week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OK for Boeing-McDonnell merger seen next week.

text.p: Regulators are likely to approve Boeing Co.'s proposed $14 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp. early next week without any major conditions, sources familiar with the situation said Friday.
Officials at the Federal Trade Commission and Boeing declined to comment.

Federal law requires the FTC's five commissioners to act within 20 days of the time the companies submit all of their materials. That would be July 1 but often in cases this complex -- between them, the two companies submitted millions of pages of supporting documents to the government -- the parties agree on an extension.

But there has been no delay in this case, where the timing is of special importance. The American decision will come as European competition authorities are reaching a crucial stage in their own review of the proposed Boeing merger.

A source familiar with negotiations between Boeing and the European Union said the airplane manufacturer has shown flexibility about changing its exclusive sales agreements with Delta Airlines, American Airlines and Continental Airlines.

Critics have called those agreements anti-competitive, saying they place the European aircraft maker Airbus Industrie at a disadvantage. After a merger, Airbus would be the only company other than Boeing to make large passenger planes.

If the agreements are changed it would remove a major roadblock in the way of EU approval. EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said this spring the merger could not be approved if Boeing's exclusive provider agreements were in place.

Whatever agreement is reached is likely to be completed next week. On July 4, EU competition authorities share their proposed recommendations on the Boeing deal in a closed meeting with competition authorities from the 15 EU nations.
Critics of the merger suggested that the Douglas division of McDonnell Douglas had served as a brake on the price of commercial airplanes and that its removal would help send prices up.
But an American analyst said that the Douglas Airplane Co. division was in severe trouble.

"The good news is that we keep the McDonnell Douglas production lines and the jobs in the United States," said Darryl Jenkins of the Consultancy Aviation Foundation in Falls Church, Va. He said that McDonnell Douglas had lost important military contracts and now had only a tiny percentage of new commercial airplane sales.
"I think Boeing has good use for the Douglas production space because Boeing is going strong," he said.
Boeing stock rose 25 cents to $54 and McDonnell Douglas gained 50 cents to $68.56 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.
